prompt: Explain what a database index is and when adding one makes writes slower, for someone who has only used spreadsheets.
text:
A database index is a separate, sorted lookup list that the database keeps alongside your data so it can find rows quickly.

**The spreadsheet version**

Say you have a sheet with a million rows of customers, and you want the row for the email "ana@example.com". Without help, you have to scan down the column from the top until you hit it. A database does the same thing when there is no index: it reads every row. That is slow when the table is large.

Now imagine you make a second sheet that holds only two columns: email, sorted alphabetically, and the row number where that customer lives in the main sheet. Because it is sorted, you can jump to the middle, see whether "ana" comes before or after, and halve the search each time (this is how a dictionary lookup works). A million rows take about twenty steps instead of a million. Then you use the row number to go straight to the full record.

That second sheet is an index. Databases build and store it for you, and they use it automatically when a query would benefit.

**Why writes get slower**

The index is a copy of part of your data, and the database has to keep it correct and sorted. So every time you change the main table, the database also has to update each index on it:

- **Insert a row:** the new email must be placed in the right spot in the sorted list, not just added at the bottom. That is extra work for every index.
- **Delete a row:** its entry must be removed from every index.
- **Update a value in an indexed column:** the old entry is removed and a new one is placed in its sorted position. Updating a column that is not indexed costs nothing extra.

If a table has five indexes, one insert is really six writes: one to the table and one to each index. The index also takes up disk space and memory.

**When it matters most**

- **Tables with many indexes.** Each one adds cost to every write.
- **Write-heavy workloads,** such as logging events or recording sensor readings, where you insert thousands of rows per second and rarely look anything up.
- **Frequently changing indexed columns.** A "last seen" timestamp that updates constantly forces constant re-sorting if you index it.
- **Bulk loads.** Importing millions of rows is often faster if you drop the indexes first and rebuild them afterward, since sorting once is cheaper than adjusting the list on every row.

**The rule of thumb**

Add an index on columns you often search, filter, or join on, in tables that are read much more than they are written. Skip it on columns you rarely search, and be sparing on tables that take heavy writes. Indexes trade slower writes and more storage for faster reads, so it is worth it only when the reads you speed up are the ones that matter.
